notes:
1. Meaning of Parliament

  • Parliament is the supreme legislative body of the Union.

It performs functions such as:

  • Making laws.
  • Amending and repealing laws.
  • Approving taxation.
  • Authorising Government expenditure.
  • Holding the Executive accountable.
  • Representing the people.
  • Discussing matters of national importance.
  • Parliament is the central institution of India's Parliamentary Democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Parliament → National Legislature + Financial Controller + Executive Watchdog

2. Constitutional Framework

Parliament is dealt with in:

  • Part V — The Union.
  • Chapter II — Parliament.
  • Articles 79–122.
  • Article 79 establishes Parliament for the Union.
📌 Must-Memorise

Union Legislature → Part V → Chapter II → Articles 79–122

3. Article 79

Parliament consists of:

  • President.
  • Rajya Sabha — Council of States.
  • Lok Sabha — House of the People.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 79 → President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha

4. Why President Is Part of Parliament

Although the President is not a member of either House, the President is an integral part of Parliament because the President:

  • Summons Parliament.
  • Prorogues Parliament.
  • May dissolve Lok Sabha.
  • Addresses Parliament.
  • Gives assent to Bills.
  • May promulgate Ordinances when Parliament is not in session.
  • The legislative process is constitutionally incomplete without Presidential participation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

President → Part of Parliament

President → Not Member of Either House

5. Bicameral Legislature

India has two Houses:

  • Rajya Sabha → Upper House.
  • Lok Sabha → Lower House.

Rajya Sabha represents:

  • States.
  • Certain Union Territories.

Lok Sabha represents:

  • People through direct election.

6. Reasons for Bicameralism

Two Houses provide:

  • Better legislative scrutiny.
  • Representation of States.
  • Wider discussion.
  • Check against hasty legislation.
  • Continuity in law-making.
  • Federal balance.

7. Parliament and Responsible Government

  • India follows a Parliamentary system.
  • Council of Ministers remains in office only while enjoying Lok Sabha confidence.

Parliament therefore ensures:

  • Responsible government.
  • Executive accountability.
  • Democratic control.

8. Legislative Functions

Parliament:

  • Enacts laws.
  • Amends laws.
  • Repeals laws.
  • Codifies legal principles.
  • Legislates on Union List.
  • Legislates on Concurrent List.
  • May legislate on State List in specified constitutional circumstances.

9. Financial Functions

Parliament:

  • Approves Union Budget.
  • Authorises taxation.
  • Authorises public expenditure.
  • Exercises financial control over Executive.
  • Examines Government accounts through Parliamentary Committees.

10. Executive Control

Important mechanisms include:

  • Question Hour.
  • Zero Hour.
  • Motions.
  • Debates.
  • Discussions.
  • Parliamentary Committees.
  • No-Confidence Motion.
  • Censure Motion.
  • Calling Attention mechanism.

11. Constitutional Functions

Parliament participates in:

  • Constitutional Amendments.
  • Election of President.
  • Election of Vice-President.
  • Impeachment of President.
  • Removal of Vice-President.
  • Removal of Judges.
  • Approval of Emergency proclamations.

12. Deliberative and Electoral Functions

Parliament:

  • Discusses public policy.
  • Discusses grievances.
  • Debates national issues.
  • Elects Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
  • Elects Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.

13. Parliament Is Not Legally Sovereign

Unlike the British Parliament, Indian Parliament is limited by:

  • Constitution.
  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Judicial Review.
  • Federal distribution of powers.
  • Basic Structure Doctrine.
📌 Must-Memorise

United Kingdom → Parliamentary Sovereignty

India → Constitutional Supremacy

14. Parliament and Federalism

  • Parliament primarily legislates on Union List.
  • It also legislates on Concurrent List.
  • It may legislate on State List under specified constitutional circumstances.

Important enabling Articles include:

  • Article 249.
  • Article 250.
  • Article 252.
  • Article 253.

15. Rajya Sabha — Constitutional Position

  • Rajya Sabha is the Upper House.

It is also known as:

  • Council of States.

It represents:

  • States.
  • Certain Union Territories.
  • It is a permanent House and cannot be dissolved.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajya Sabha → Council of States → Permanent House

16. Rajya Sabha — Important Articles

Important Articles include:

  • Article 80 → Composition.
  • Article 84 → Qualifications.
  • Article 89 → Chairman and Deputy Chairman.
  • Articles 107–111 → Legislative procedure.
  • Article 249 → Parliament on State List in national interest.
  • Article 312 → Creation of All India Services.

17. Rajya Sabha — Maximum Strength

Article 80 permits a maximum strength of:

  • 250 members.

This includes:

  • Up to 238 representatives of States and Union Territories.
  • Up to 12 nominated members.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajya Sabha Maximum → 250

Elected/Representatives → Up to 238

Nominated → 12

18. Rajya Sabha — Present Strength in the Reference

The attached notes record:

  • Present sanctioned strength → 245.
  • Elected members → 233.
  • Nominated members → 12.

19. Election of State Representatives to Rajya Sabha

State representatives are:

  • Indirectly elected.
  • Elected by elected members of State Legislative Assemblies.

Election uses:

  • Proportional Representation.
  • Single Transferable Vote.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajya Sabha Election → Elected MLAs → PR + STV

20. Union Territory Representation in Rajya Sabha

  • Only specified Union Territories receive Rajya Sabha representation.
  • Representation is determined through parliamentary law.
  • Not every Union Territory has Rajya Sabha seats.

21. Nominated Members of Rajya Sabha

President nominates 12 members having special knowledge or practical experience in:

  • Literature.
  • Science.
  • Art.
  • Social Service.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajya Sabha Nominations → 12

Fields → Literature + Science + Art + Social Service

22. Unequal State Representation

  • Rajya Sabha seats are not equally distributed among States.
  • Larger States generally receive more seats than smaller States.
  • This differs from the United States Senate, where States have equal representation.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rajya Sabha → Equal State Representation? → No

23. Rajya Sabha Qualifications

Under Article 84, a member must:

  • Be an Indian citizen.
  • Make prescribed oath or affirmation.
  • Possess qualifications prescribed by Parliament.
  • Be at least 30 years of age.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajya Sabha Minimum Age → 30 Years

24. Rajya Sabha Disqualification

Disqualification may arise under:

  • Article 102.
  • Representation of the People Act, 1951.
  • Tenth Schedule.

25. Rajya Sabha Term

  • Rajya Sabha is never dissolved.

Each member normally serves:

  • Six years.
  • Approximately one-third retire every two years.
  • Fresh elections fill the resulting vacancies.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajya Sabha Member → 6 Years

1/3 Retire → Every 2 Years

26. Chairman of Rajya Sabha

  • Vice-President of India is the ex-officio Chairman.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 64.
  • Chairman presides over proceedings.

27. Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha

  • Rajya Sabha elects one of its members as Deputy Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman presides when Chairman is absent.

28. Rajya Sabha Quorum

Quorum is:

  • One-tenth of total membership.

If quorum is absent, proceedings may be:

  • Adjourned.
  • Suspended until quorum is available.
📌 Must-Memorise

Parliamentary Quorum → 1/10 of Total Membership

29. Rajya Sabha and Ordinary Bills

Rajya Sabha may:

  • Introduce Ordinary Bills.
  • Debate them.
  • Pass them.
  • Reject them.
  • Suggest amendments.
  • For Ordinary Bills, both Houses ordinarily have equal powers.

30. Rajya Sabha and Money Bills

A Money Bill:

  • Cannot be introduced in Rajya Sabha.
  • Can only be recommended upon by Rajya Sabha.
  • Must be returned within 14 days.
  • Lok Sabha may accept or reject recommendations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Money Bill → Rajya Sabha → 14 Days + Recommendations Only

31. Rajya Sabha and Constitutional Amendment Bills

  • Rajya Sabha has equal power with Lok Sabha.
  • Amendment Bill must pass separately in both Houses.
  • No Joint Sitting is permitted.

32. Article 249

Rajya Sabha may authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject if:

  • Resolution declares legislation necessary in national interest.

Resolution is supported by:

  • Not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 249 → Rajya Sabha → State List → National Interest → 2/3 Present & Voting

33. Article 312

Rajya Sabha may authorise creation of one or more All India Services by resolution supported by:

  • Not less than two-thirds of members present and voting.
  • Resolution must declare such creation necessary in national interest.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 312 → Rajya Sabha → New All India Services

34. All India Services Examples

Examples mentioned in the notes:

  • IAS.
  • IPS.
  • Indian Forest Service.

35. Rajya Sabha during Emergency

  • Rajya Sabha continues even when Lok Sabha stands dissolved.
  • This maintains continuity of Parliament during exceptional periods.

36. Lok Sabha — Constitutional Position

  • Lok Sabha is the Lower House.

It is also known as:

  • House of the People.
  • It directly represents citizens.

It is:

  • Directly elected.
  • Subject to dissolution.

It has a dominant position in:

  • Executive responsibility.
  • Financial matters.

37. Lok Sabha — Important Articles

  • Article 81 → Composition.
  • Article 83 → Duration.
  • Article 84 → Qualifications.
  • Article 85 → Sessions.
  • Article 93 → Speaker and Deputy Speaker.
  • Articles 107–111 → Legislative procedure.
  • Article 110 → Money Bills.

38. Lok Sabha Composition

  • Article 81 provides for members directly elected from territorial constituencies.

Representation is broadly connected with:

  • Population.
  • Territorial constituencies.

The attached notes record present sanctioned strength as:

  • 543 elected members.

39. Anglo-Indian Nomination

  • Constitution originally permitted nomination of Anglo-Indian members to Lok Sabha under Article 331.
  • The attached notes state that this provision was abolished by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019, effective from 2020.
  • Lok Sabha therefore consists only of elected members under the framework described in the attachment.
📌 Must-Memorise

104th Amendment → Anglo-Indian Nomination to Lok Sabha Ended

40. Lok Sabha Election

Members are elected through:

  • Direct election.
  • Universal Adult Franchise.
  • First-Past-The-Post system.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lok Sabha → Direct Election + FPTP

41. Voting Eligibility

A citizen generally must:

  • Be 18 years or above.
  • Be registered as an elector.
  • Not be disqualified under law.

42. First-Past-The-Post System

  • Each constituency elects one member.
  • Candidate obtaining the highest number of valid votes is declared elected.
  • Absolute majority is not necessary.

43. Parliamentary Constituencies

  • India is divided into Parliamentary constituencies.
  • Each constituency elects one Lok Sabha member.
  • Delimitation Commission redraws boundaries according to constitutional and statutory provisions.

44. Lok Sabha Qualifications

A candidate must:

  • Be a citizen of India.
  • Make prescribed oath or affirmation.
  • Possess qualifications prescribed by Parliament.
  • Be at least 25 years old.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lok Sabha Minimum Age → 25 Years

45. Lok Sabha Term

Normal term:

  • Five years from date appointed for first sitting.
  • Lok Sabha may be dissolved before expiry.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 83 → Lok Sabha → 5 Years

46. Extension during National Emergency

During National Emergency:

Parliament may extend Lok Sabha's term:

  • One year at a time.

Extension cannot continue beyond:

  • Six months after Emergency ceases.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Emergency Extension → 1 Year at a Time

Maximum Beyond End of Emergency → 6 Months

47. Dissolution of Lok Sabha

Lok Sabha may end:

  • By Presidential dissolution on advice of Prime Minister.
  • On expiry of normal term, unless constitutionally extended during National Emergency.

48. Exclusive Executive-Control Power of Lok Sabha

  • Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to Lok Sabha.

Lok Sabha may remove Government through:

  • No-Confidence Motion.
  • Rajya Sabha cannot remove Government through a no-confidence vote.

49. Exclusive Financial Position of Lok Sabha

Money Bills:

  • Originate only in Lok Sabha.
  • Require prior Presidential recommendation.
  • Are certified by Speaker.
  • Rajya Sabha has only recommendatory powers.

50. Electoral Functions of Lok Sabha

Lok Sabha participates in:

  • Presidential election through elected members.
  • Vice-Presidential election through Members of Parliament.
  • Election of Speaker.
  • Election of Deputy Speaker.

51. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — Ordinary Bills

  • Both Houses ordinarily have equal legislative powers.
  • Deadlock may result in Joint Sitting under Article 108 where applicable.

52. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — Amendment Bills

  • Both Houses possess equal powers.
  • Each must separately pass the Amendment Bill.
  • No Joint Sitting.

53. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha — Money Bills

Lok Sabha:

  • Dominant.

Rajya Sabha:

  • Recommendation only.
  • 14-day limit.

54. Article 84 — Parliamentary Qualifications

Article 84 requires:

  • Citizenship of India.
  • Prescribed oath or affirmation.
  • Required age.
  • Other qualifications prescribed by Parliament.

55. Parliamentary Oath

Article 99 requires each member to take prescribed oath or affirmation before:

  • Sitting.
  • Participating.
  • Voting.
  • Form of oath is contained in Third Schedule.

56. Age Requirement

  • Lok Sabha → 25 years.
  • Rajya Sabha → 30 years.
📌 Must-Memorise

LS → 25

RS → 30

57. Representation of the People Act, 1951

The Act supplements constitutional qualifications and disqualifications.

A candidate should:

  • Be a registered elector.
  • Complete valid nomination requirements.
  • Satisfy statutory conditions.
  • Be free from statutory disqualification.

58. Article 102 — Disqualification

A person may be disqualified because of:

  • Office of Profit.
  • Unsound mind declared by competent court.
  • Undischarged insolvency.
  • Loss of Indian citizenship.
  • Voluntary acquisition of foreign citizenship.
  • Acknowledgement of allegiance to foreign State.
  • Disqualification under parliamentary law.

59. Office of Profit

Purpose of office-of-profit disqualification:

  • Maintain legislative independence.
  • Prevent executive influence.
  • Prevent conflicts between Legislature and Executive.
  • Constitution does not define the expression exhaustively in the attached notes.

60. Statutory Disqualifications

Representation of the People Act may disqualify for reasons including:

  • Conviction for specified offences.
  • Corrupt electoral practices.
  • Failure to submit election expenditure accounts.
  • Certain prohibited Government contracts or offices.
  • Other statutory grounds.

61. Article 101 — Double Membership

A person cannot simultaneously remain:

  • Member of both Houses of Parliament.
  • Member of Parliament and State Legislature.

One seat must be vacated according to law.

62. Resignation of Members

Lok Sabha member:

  • Resignation addressed to Speaker.

Rajya Sabha member:

  • Resignation addressed to Chairman.

Presiding Officer must be satisfied that resignation is:

  • Voluntary.
  • Genuine.

63. Absence for Sixty Days

House may declare seat vacant if a member is absent without permission for:

  • 60 consecutive days.

Periods when House is:

  • Prorogued, or
  • Adjourned for more than four consecutive days

are excluded from computation.

📌 Must-Memorise

Unauthorised Absence → 60 Days

64. Article 103 — Decision on Disqualification

  • President decides questions relating to disqualification of Members of Parliament.

Before deciding:

  • President must obtain Election Commission's opinion.
  • President acts according to that opinion.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 103 → President + Election Commission Opinion

65. Sessions of Parliament

A session:

  • Begins with first sitting after summoning.
  • Ends with prorogation.

Contains:

  • Several sittings.
  • Adjournments.
  • Recesses.

66. Article 85 — Summoning

  • President summons each House.
  • President acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers.

67. Maximum Gap between Sessions

Not more than six months may intervene between:

  • Last sitting of one session.
  • First sitting of next session.
  • Parliament must therefore meet at least twice every year.
📌 Must-Memorise

Maximum Gap → 6 Months

68. Usual Parliamentary Sessions

Parliament generally follows:

  • Budget Session.
  • Monsoon Session.
  • Winter Session.
  • These names are based on parliamentary practice, not constitutional terminology.

69. Budget Session

Usually:

  • January/February to April/May.

Major business includes:

  • President's Address.
  • Union Budget.
  • Finance legislation.
  • Demands for Grants.
  • Major Bills.
  • It is generally the longest session.

70. Monsoon and Winter Sessions

Monsoon Session generally includes:

  • Legislative business.
  • Discussions.
  • Questions.
  • Committee reports.

Winter Session generally deals with:

  • Pending legislation.
  • Supplementary demands.
  • Current national issues.

71. Meaning of Sitting

  • Sitting means a single day's meeting of a House.
  • One session consists of multiple sittings.

72. Adjournment

Adjournment means temporary suspension of a sitting for:

  • Hours.
  • One day.
  • Several days.

Authority:

  • Speaker in Lok Sabha.
  • Chairman in Rajya Sabha.
  • Session itself continues.

73. Adjournment Sine Die

  • House is adjourned without fixing date for next sitting.

Ordered by:

  • Speaker.
  • Chairman.
  • Session technically continues until prorogation.
📌 Must-Memorise

Adjournment Sine Die → No Date Fixed

74. Prorogation

  • Prorogation formally ends an entire session.
  • President prorogues the House under Article 85 on ministerial advice.

It:

  • Ends session.
  • Does not dissolve House.
  • Does not ordinarily terminate pending Bills.
  • Does not normally stop committee work.

75. Dissolution

  • Dissolution ends the existence of Lok Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved.

After dissolution:

  • Lok Sabha members cease to hold office.
  • General election becomes necessary.

76. Effect of Lok Sabha Dissolution on Bills

Bill pending in Lok Sabha:

  • Lapses.

Bill passed by Lok Sabha but pending in Rajya Sabha:

  • Lapses.

Bill pending in Rajya Sabha but not passed by Lok Sabha:

  • Does not lapse.

Constitutional Amendment Bill:

  • Does not lapse merely because Lok Sabha is dissolved, according to the attached notes.

77. Article 87 — President's Special Address

President addresses:

  • First session after every General Election.
  • First session of every year.

Address outlines:

  • Government policies.
  • Legislative programme.
  • National priorities.
  • Both Houses discuss Motion of Thanks.

78. Article 86

President may:

  • Address either House.
  • Address both Houses together.
  • Send messages to either House.

79. Article 88

Ministers and Attorney General may:

  • Speak in either House.
  • Participate in proceedings.
  • Participate in committees where entitled.

They cannot vote unless they are members of that House.

80. Adjournment vs Prorogation vs Dissolution

Adjournment:

  • Suspends sitting.
  • Speaker/Chairman.
  • Session continues.
  • Applies to both Houses.

Prorogation:

  • Ends session.
  • President.
  • House continues.
  • Applies to both Houses.

Dissolution:

  • Ends Lok Sabha itself.
  • President or expiry of term.
  • Applies only to Lok Sabha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Adjournment → Sitting

Prorogation → Session

Dissolution → Lok Sabha

81. Article 93 — Speaker and Deputy Speaker

Lok Sabha elects:

  • Speaker.
  • Deputy Speaker

from among its members.

82. Speaker's Oath

  • Speaker does not take a separate oath as Speaker.
  • Speaker functions after taking oath as Member of Parliament.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Separate Speaker Oath → No

83. Speaker's Term after Dissolution

  • Speaker continues even after Lok Sabha dissolution.
  • Continues until immediately before first meeting of newly elected Lok Sabha.
  • This ensures continuity.

84. Speaker's Resignation

Speaker resigns to:

  • Deputy Speaker.
📌 Must-Memorise

Speaker Resignation → Deputy Speaker

85. Removal of Speaker

  • Removal by resolution of Lok Sabha.

Majority required:

  • Majority of all the then members of Lok Sabha.

Notice:

  • 14 days.

86. Speaker during Removal Motion

While removal resolution is under consideration:

  • Speaker cannot preside.
  • Speaker may participate.
  • Speaker may vote as an ordinary member.

87. Speaker's Main Powers

Speaker:

  • Presides over sittings.
  • Maintains order.
  • Regulates debate.
  • Interprets procedural rules.
  • Preserves discipline.
  • Certifies Money Bills.
  • Exercises casting vote.
  • Presides over Joint Sitting.
  • Exercises committee-related functions.
  • Decides defection questions for Lok Sabha.
  • Heads Lok Sabha Secretariat.

88. Money Bill Certification

  • Under Article 110, Speaker decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill.
  • Certification accompanies Bill when sent to Rajya Sabha.
  • It has major constitutional significance.

89. Speaker's Voting Power

  • Speaker does not vote in first instance.
  • Speaker votes only when votes are equally divided.

Such vote is called:

  • Casting Vote.

90. Speaker and Joint Sitting

Under Article 108, order of presiding officers is:

  • Speaker of Lok Sabha.
  • Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha.
  • Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
  • Other person determined according to applicable rules.
  • Chairman of Rajya Sabha does not preside.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Joint Sitting Chair → Speaker

Vice-President/RS Chairman → Does Not Preside

91. Deputy Speaker

  • Elected by Lok Sabha from among its members.
  • Presides when Speaker is absent.
  • Exercises Speaker's powers while presiding.
  • Resigns to Speaker.
  • Removal requires majority of all then members of Lok Sabha.

92. Rajya Sabha Presiding Officers

Rajya Sabha has:

  • Chairman.
  • Deputy Chairman.

Chairman:

  • Vice-President of India.
  • Ex-officio.
  • Not elected by Rajya Sabha.

Deputy Chairman:

  • Elected by Rajya Sabha from among its members.

93. Chairman's Voting

Rajya Sabha Chairman:

  • Does not vote in first instance.
  • Has casting vote in case of equality.

94. Speaker vs Rajya Sabha Chairman

Speaker:

  • Lok Sabha.
  • Elected by House.
  • Member of Lok Sabha.
  • Certifies Money Bills.
  • Presides over Joint Sitting.

Chairman:

  • Rajya Sabha.
  • Vice-President automatically becomes Chairman.
  • Not member of Rajya Sabha.
  • No Money Bill certification.
  • Does not preside over Joint Sitting.

95. Ordinary Bill

An Ordinary Bill is a Bill that is not:

  • Money Bill.
  • Financial Bill.
  • Constitutional Amendment Bill.

It deals with general matters within Parliament's legislative competence.

96. Who May Introduce an Ordinary Bill

It may be introduced by:

  • Minister.
  • Private Member.

It may originate in:

  • Lok Sabha.
  • Rajya Sabha.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ordinary Bill → Either House → Minister or Private Member

97. First Reading

  • Bill is introduced.
  • Detailed discussion usually does not occur at this stage.
  • Publication in Official Gazette may follow according to procedure.

98. Second Reading

Second Reading includes:

  • General Discussion.
  • Committee Stage.
  • Consideration Stage.

It is the most detailed stage of legislative scrutiny.

99. Committee Stage of a Bill

Bill may be referred to:

  • Department-related Standing Committee.
  • Select Committee.
  • Joint Committee.

Committee may examine:

  • Clauses.
  • Expert views.
  • Public representations.
  • Administrative implications.

100. Consideration Stage

House considers Bill:

  • Clause by clause.
  • Members may move amendments.
  • Amendments may be accepted or rejected.
  • Clauses are voted upon.

101. Third Reading

  • Debate is limited.
  • Focus is whether Bill should finally pass.
  • If passed, Bill goes to other House.

102. Other House's Options

Second House may:

  • Pass Bill.
  • Reject Bill.
  • Amend Bill.
  • Keep Bill pending.

If both Houses agree on identical text:

  • Bill goes to President.

103. Article 111 — President and Ordinary Bill

President may:

  • Give assent.
  • Withhold assent in limited circumstances.
  • Return an Ordinary Bill once.

If Parliament passes it again:

  • President must assent.

104. Money Bill — Article 110

A Money Bill contains only matters specified in Article 110(1).

📌 Must-Memorise

Money Bill → Article 110

105. Article 110 — Tax Matters

Money Bill may deal with:

  • Imposition of tax.
  • Abolition of tax.
  • Remission.
  • Alteration.
  • Regulation of tax.

106. Government Borrowing

Money Bill may deal with:

  • Government borrowing.
  • Government guarantees.
  • Laws relating to Government financial obligations.

107. Consolidated and Contingency Funds

Money Bill may deal with:

  • Custody of Consolidated Fund.
  • Custody of Contingency Fund.
  • Payments into those Funds.
  • Withdrawals from those Funds.

108. Appropriation and Charged Expenditure

Money Bill may deal with:

  • Appropriation from Consolidated Fund.
  • Declaring expenditure charged on Consolidated Fund.
  • Increasing charged expenditure.

109. Receipt, Public Account and Audit

Money Bill may contain provisions concerning:

  • Receipt of money into Consolidated Fund.
  • Public Account.
  • Custody of Government money.
  • Audit of Union accounts.
  • Matters incidental to Article 110 subjects.

110. Matters That Do Not Alone Make a Money Bill

A Bill is not a Money Bill merely because it provides for:

  • Fines.
  • Penalties.
  • Licence fees.
  • Fees for services.
  • Local taxation by local authorities.

111. Money Bill Introduction

  • Only in Lok Sabha.
  • Only by a Minister according to the attached notes.
  • Prior recommendation of President is mandatory.

112. Role of Rajya Sabha in Money Bill

Rajya Sabha:

  • Cannot reject.
  • Cannot amend.
  • May recommend.
  • Must return within 14 days.

Lok Sabha:

  • May accept or reject recommendations.

113. Money Bill Not Returned in 14 Days

If Rajya Sabha does not return within 14 days:

  • Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in form passed by Lok Sabha.

114. Money Bill and President

  • President may assent.
  • President cannot return Money Bill for reconsideration under Article 111.

115. No Joint Sitting for Money Bill

  • Article 108 Joint Sitting is not available.

Reason:

  • Rajya Sabha does not have equal legislative authority over Money Bills.

116. Money Bill vs Financial Bill

  • Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill.
  • Every Financial Bill is not a Money Bill.
📌 Must-Memorise

Money Bill ⊂ Financial Bills

117. Financial Bill Category I

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 117(1).

It:

  • Contains one or more Article 110 matters.
  • Also contains other ordinary provisions.
  • Is therefore not a Money Bill.

118. Category I Procedure

According to the attached notes:

  • Introduced only in Lok Sabha.
  • Introduced by Minister.
  • Prior Presidential recommendation required.
  • Rajya Sabha has equal legislative power.
  • Joint Sitting is possible in case of deadlock.

119. Financial Bill Category II

184. Article 105 — Parliamentary Privileges

185. Purpose of Privileges

  • Legislative independence.

  • Freedom from improper interference.
  • Effective performance of parliamentary functions.
  • Dignity of Parliament.

186. Collective Privileges

House collectively may:

  • Regulate internal proceedings.
  • Maintain discipline.
  • Punish breach of privilege.
  • Exclude strangers.
  • Control authorised publication.
  • Conduct inquiries.
  • Summon witnesses.
  • Call for documents.

  • Constitution.

189. Civil Arrest

  • Traditional privilege provides limited protection from civil arrest during specified periods connected with parliamentary sessions.

It does not extend to:

  • Criminal arrest.
  • Preventive detention.

190. Breach of Privilege

Examples include:

  • Obstructing member's parliamentary duties.
  • Publishing distorted reports.
  • Refusing to appear before committee without valid reason.
  • Threatening members.
  • Disobeying lawful House orders.

191. Contempt of Parliament

  • Obstruct Parliament.
